sections.h2: Who taxes a Texas house and who sends the bill
sections.html:
The state itself levies no property tax. Instead the county, a school district, often a city and sometimes special districts each charge their own rate on the same home.

A separate appraisal district sets the value. Its chief appraiser values each parcel as of January 1 and handles exemption requests, and a review board hears disagreements. Many units contract with the county tax assessor-collector, who mails one combined bill in October.

The year follows a fixed schedule. These ten dates matter most to a homeowner.

Texas property tax dates for a homeowner
DateWhat happens
Jan. 1Value, exemption status and the year's tax lien are fixed
Apr. 1 or soon afterValue notices go out for single-family homesteads
Apr. 30Deadline for many exemption applications
May 1 or soon afterValue notices for other property
May 15Protest deadline, unless 30 days after the notice is later
July 25Chief appraiser certifies the roll
Sept. 29Most units adopt rates by this date, or within 60 days of the roll if later
Oct. 1Bills mailed
Nov. 30 and June 30Halves of a split payment
Jan. 31Final day without delinquency

Bills arrive in October and are payable on receipt. Delinquency begins the following February 1.

sections.h2: How a taxing unit sets its rate
sections.html:
Units follow a notice-and-hearing sequence called truth-in-taxation. Once the certified roll arrives, most units work out two benchmark rates before they vote.

The no-new-revenue rate would collect the same dollars from the same properties as last year. The voter-approval rate is the ceiling above which voters must approve. For most non-school units it lets operating revenue grow 3.5 percent over the prior year, plus room for debt service. Junior college and hospital districts and other special units get 8 percent. Going over the ceiling triggers an election on the next uniform election date.

  • Units post both benchmark rates on their homepages.
  • Each notice names when the vote will happen.
  • Units other than very small ones hold a public hearing.

Renditions concern business and other personal property more than homes. The rendition period starts January 2, and April 15 is the last day for most property types. The chief appraiser must extend to May 15 when asked in writing. A homeowner usually does not file one, but a landlord with equipment or a business owner with furnishings might.

sections.h2: When unpaid property tax turns delinquent
sections.html:
Any balance still open after January ends is delinquent the next morning. That day the collector adds six percent in penalty and one percent in interest. The penalty then grows one percent a month until it reaches twelve percent in July, and interest keeps running monthly with no ceiling.

A unit with a collection lawyer under contract may add up to a fifth more. Bills must allow 21 days, so a bill mailed after January 10 pushes delinquency later. A bill dated January 15, for example, goes delinquent March 1.

Older or disabled homeowners can pay in four installments, the first due by February 1 and the rest on March 31, May 31 and July 31. A late installment draws a six percent penalty plus one percent monthly interest.

  • A waiver of penalty and interest is possible when the owner pays within 21 days of learning about the delinquency and asks in writing before day 181.
  • Some collectors allow payment plans up to 36 months, and one is required for a residence homestead.
  • A homeowner past 65, or disabled, may pay a current bill in four installments.

sections.h2: Exemptions that lower a home's taxable value
sections.html:
The residence homestead exemption is the largest. Every school district exempts $140,000 of homestead value, and any unit may adopt a local option cut of up to 20 percent, never below $5,000.

  • Age 65 and up, or a qualifying disability, brings an added $60,000 school exemption.
  • Disabled veterans get $5,000 to $12,000 off by rating level, and the homestead of one rated 100 percent is fully exempt.
  • A surviving spouse 55 or older can in some cases keep a late spouse's over-65 benefit.

The usual filing window closes at the end of April. A buyer who closes after the first of the year can claim the exemption right away for that year if the seller had not.

sections.h2: What happens if a delinquent account goes unpaid?
sections.html:
The collection path runs from delinquent notices to an optional payment plan to a lawsuit, with court costs added to the bill. A suit can end in an auction run by a constable or a hired agent. Auctions are posted locally, so check the county clerk and tax office websites.

What a former owner can recover depends on the property type. Homestead, agricultural and mineral property carry a two-year redemption period, and a former owner has two years to claim any excess sale proceeds. Heirs who inherit a house with delinquent years should call the tax office early, since the account may qualify for a plan.

Two limits apply. A homestead's appraised value may climb at most 10 percent a year once the exemption has been in place a year, except for new improvements.

An owner past 65 or disabled also gets a school tax ceiling fixed at the year of qualifying. If the owner moves within Texas, a proportional share of the ceiling can go along. Counties, cities and junior college districts can adopt their own ceiling, so ask each unit whether it has.

sections.h2: What if the appraisal looks too high?
sections.html:
A protest goes to the appraisal review board, usually by May 15 or a month after the notice, whichever date falls later. After the board decides, appeals can go to district court, regular binding arbitration, or the State Office of Administrative Hearings when the board's value exceeds $1,000,000.

An appeal needs at least the undisputed part of the tax paid before delinquency. Our separate protest guide covers the hearing itself.

The yearly lien stays with the house, so title companies insist that old years be cleared. Whoever held title at the start of the year remains answerable for that year's tax and may be sued even after selling.

The title company usually pays delinquent amounts out of the seller's proceeds and splits the current year between the parties. Ask the assessor-collector for a tax certificate listing every unit, and confirm what the title company will show on the settlement statement.

  • Look for delinquent years, penalties and attorney fees.
  • Ask whether a payment plan exists on the account.
  • After closing, the buyer files for the homestead exemption in the buyer's name.

A seller with back taxes who wants to skip repairs, showings and a lender's timeline can look at a cash sale, since the amounts owed come out of the proceeds at closing either way.

faqs.q: Does the state of Texas collect property tax?
faqs.a: No. The state levies none, and local taxing units set rates and collect the money.

faqs.q: When must Texas property tax be paid?
faqs.a: Bills are mailed in October with payment due on arrival. Delinquency starts February 1 for anything open after January 31. Where a split payment is allowed, halves are due November 30 and June 30.

faqs.q: What is the late charge on Texas property tax?
faqs.a: Six percent penalty and one percent interest land on day one of delinquency. The penalty then climbs one percent a month to twelve percent in July.

faqs.q: How large is the Texas homestead exemption?
faqs.a: School districts must exempt $140,000, with $60,000 extra for older or disabled owners. Other units may add local exemptions.

faqs.q: Can delinquent tax be paid out of a sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Title companies usually settle it from the seller's proceeds, since the lien stays with the house.
